title: Listen or hear?
description: «Listen or hear?» – Modul 2 im Englisch-Lernpfad «Cate's Sound Lab»: Du lernst den Unterschied zwischen listen (to) und hear, übst die richtige Form in Sätzen aus der Welt von Songs und Radio – und erzählst mit past simple und past perfect, was an einem Konzertabend zuerst passierte. Niveau A2–B1 (9. Schulstufe).
subject: E
einheit: Cate's Sound Lab – über Musik sprechen
learningObjectives: I can use listen (to) and hear correctly. (Ich kann listen (to) und hear richtig verwenden.)
I can form and use the past perfect for the earlier of two past actions. (Ich kann das past perfect bilden und für die frühere von zwei vergangenen Handlungen verwenden.)
I can decide which of two past actions happened first and choose the right tense. (Ich kann entscheiden, welche von zwei vergangenen Handlungen zuerst passierte, und die passende Zeitform wählen.)

blocks.title: Welcome back to «Cate's Sound Lab»!
blocks.body:
In Module 1 you talked about your music taste. In this second module you will practise two things that English learners often mix up:

- **Part 1 – two verbs for your ears:** When do you use *listen (to)*, and when do you use *hear*?
- **Part 2 – two past tenses:** How do you show that one thing in the past happened **before** another thing? This is the job of the *past perfect*.

All examples come from the world of songs, concerts and radio. Read the two short explanations carefully – then the exercises will feel much easier.

blocks.title: Part 1: listen or hear – what is the difference?
blocks.body:
**listen = active.** You decide to do it, and you give the music your attention.

- Cate puts on her headphones and **listens to** her new playlist.
- Please **listen** carefully – the melody changes after the chorus.

**hear = passive.** It just happens. The sound comes to your ears, and you did not plan it.

- On my way to school I sometimes **hear** music from an open window.
- Did you **hear** that? Somebody is playing the drums!

**The little word *to*:** Before an object, *listen* always needs **to**: you listen **to** music, you listen **to** the radio. *Hear* never takes *to*: you simply hear a sound. And when there is no object at all, *listen* stands alone: «Quiet, please – now listen!»

Look at the picture: the girl has chosen her music and gives it her attention. The boy did not choose anything – the song simply reaches his ears.

blocks.title: Listen or hear?
blocks.alt: Chart with two halves. Left half, blue, titled «LISTEN (+ to)»: a girl with big headphones and closed eyes enjoys music; notes float around her head. Below: «active – you decide to do it», with the example «She listens TO her playlist.» and the reminder «with an object you always need to». Right half, orange, titled «HEAR»: a boy walks past a house; music notes come out of an open window and reach his ears. Below: «passive – it just happens», with the example «He hears music from a window.» and the reminder «never with to». A dark bar at the bottom sums it up: listen to music – correct; listen music – wrong; hear a sound – no to.
blocks.caption: Left: you choose the music and give it your attention. Right: the sound just comes to your ears – you did not plan it.

blocks.title: Exercise 1: listen, listen to or hear?
blocks.intro: Choose the correct word or words for each gap. Think: active or passive? And do you need *to*?

questions.prompt: Every morning I turn on the radio and ___ my favourite programme while I eat breakfast.
questions.explanation: You turn on the radio yourself and choose the programme – that is active, so you need *listen*. And because *my favourite programme* is an object, *to* must come before it: «I listen to my favourite programme.» *Listen* without *to* is wrong here, and *hear to* does not exist.

questions.prompt: Our walls are very thin. I often ___ my neighbour's music, even when my door is closed.
questions.explanation: The music comes through the wall – you did not choose it, it just happens. That is passive: *hear*. *Listen (to)* would mean you give the neighbour's music your full attention on purpose. And after *I*, the verb has no -s, so *hears* is wrong.

questions.prompt: Stop talking and ___ carefully – I will play the song only once.
questions.explanation: This is active – you should give the song your full attention. There is no object after the gap, only the adverb *carefully*, so *listen* stands alone without *to*. *Hear carefully* is not used in English, because you cannot control hearing.

questions.prompt: My brother ___ his favourite band every day – always with his big headphones on.
questions.explanation: Headphones on, every day, his choice – that is active. With an object (*his favourite band*) you need *to*: «He listens to his favourite band.» *Listens* without *to* is the classic trap, and after *my brother* the verb needs its -s, so *listen to* is wrong too.

questions.prompt: Did you ___ that? I think someone just shouted your name near the stage!
questions.explanation: The shout came suddenly – nobody planned to give it attention. That is passive: *hear*. And after *did you …?* the verb must be in its base form, so *listening* does not work.

blocks.title: Exercise 2: Type the correct form
blocks.intro: Type the correct form of *listen (to)* or *hear* into each gap. Pay attention to the time in each sentence – some are about the past. And don't forget *to* where it is needed.
blocks.text:

Our neighbours are loud. Even with my door closed, I {{2}} their music through the wall.
Yesterday, while I was doing my homework, I suddenly {{3}} a great new song on the radio.
Last night we sat down and {{4}} the whole album from start to finish.
My grandad turns on the radio and {{5}} his favourite station every morning.
The music in this café is very quiet – can you {{6}} it at all?

blocks.title: Part 2: past simple or past perfect – which happened first?
blocks.body:
Read this sentence from a concert evening:

> When we **arrived**, the band **had** already **started**.

Two things happened in the past – but not at the same time. First the band started, then we arrived. English shows this order with two tenses:

- **past perfect** for the **earlier** action: *the band **had started***
- **past simple** for the **later** action: *we **arrived***

**The form is easy:** **had + past participle** – and it stays the same for I, you, he, she, it, we and they. *I had heard – she had heard – they had heard.*

**Signal words** that often appear in these sentences: *before, after, already, by the time, when*.

**Six past participles you will need – learn them by heart:**

| verb | past simple | past participle |
|---|---|---|
| go | went | gone |
| see | saw | seen |
| hear | heard | heard |
| sing | sang | sung |
| buy | bought | bought |
| begin | began | begun |

The timeline picture shows the concert example: both actions lie in the past, but one of them lies further back.

blocks.title: The timeline: past perfect and past simple
blocks.alt: Timeline chart. A long arrow runs from left to right and ends at a dark marker labelled «NOW». Two dots sit on the timeline in the past. The earlier dot, on the left, is blue and labelled «1st – earlier action: past perfect», with the example «The band had started.» The later dot, further right, is orange and labelled «2nd – later action: past simple», with the example «We arrived.» A curved arrow points from the later dot back to the earlier dot. Below the timeline, the full example sentence reads «When we arrived, the band had already started.» A dark bar at the bottom shows the rule: past perfect = had + past participle, the same for all persons.
blocks.caption: Both actions are in the past – the past perfect marks the one that happened first.

blocks.title: Exercise 3: Which action came first?
blocks.intro: Five questions in two formats: sometimes you decide which action happened first, sometimes you choose the correct form for a gap.

questions.prompt: «When Lena arrived at the hall, the concert had already begun.» – What happened first?

options.text: Both happened at the same time.
The sentence does not tell us.

questions.explanation: *Had begun* is past perfect – the tense for the earlier of two past actions. So the concert began first, and Lena arrived later. The word *already* is an extra signal for «before that».

questions.prompt: «By the time we reached the hall, the first song ___.»
questions.explanation: *By the time* tells you: one past action was already complete when the other happened. The earlier, completed action takes the past perfect: *had finished*. *Has finished* is the present perfect and does not fit a story about the past, and *finishes* is present tense.

questions.prompt: «The DJ played a song that I had heard on the radio many times before.» – What happened first?

options.text: I heard the song on the radio.
Both happened at the same time.
The sentence does not tell us.

questions.explanation: *Had heard* is past perfect, so the hearing on the radio came first – many times, in fact. Then, later, the DJ played the song. *Before* is the signal word here.

questions.prompt: «When we ___ the hall, the band had already played three songs.»
questions.explanation: The three songs came first – that is why they are in the past perfect. Our arrival is the later action, and the later action takes the past simple: *entered*. Two past perfects in one sentence would not show which action was first.

questions.prompt: «The singer was not nervous, because she ___ the song hundreds of times before that evening.»
questions.explanation: The singing happened before that evening – the earlier action takes the past perfect: *had + past participle*. The participle of *sing* is *sung*, so *had sang* is a trap. *Has sung* is present perfect, and *sings* is present tense.

blocks.title: Exercise 4: A concert evening
blocks.intro: Drag the verb forms into the story (on a phone: tap the form first, then the gap). **Watch out: three forms in the list are wrong forms – they fit nowhere.**
blocks.text:

By the time we found our seats, the support band {{5}} its show, and the stage was empty.

I {{7}} the album so many times at home! It was a fantastic night.

blocks.title: Final quiz: listen, hear and the past perfect
blocks.intro: Five questions from both parts of the module. You can go back and read the explanations again at any time.

questions.prompt: You are on the bus. Someone's phone plays loud music – you don't want it, but you ___ it anyway.
questions.explanation: You did not choose this music – it simply reaches your ears. That is passive: *hear*. *Listen (to)* would mean you give it your attention on purpose, and *hear to* does not exist.

options.text: I often listen music in my room.
I often listen at music in my room.
I often hear to music in my room.
I often listen to music in my room.

questions.explanation: Before an object, *listen* always needs *to*: «listen to music». *Listen music* and *listen at music* are wrong, and *hear* never takes *to*.

questions.prompt: How do you form the past perfect?
questions.explanation: The past perfect is *had + past participle*, and it stays the same for all persons: I had heard, she had heard, they had heard. *Have/has + past participle* is the present perfect – a different tense.

questions.prompt: «When the radio show ended, I had already ordered the band's new album.» – What happened first?

options.text: Both happened at the same time.

questions.explanation: *Had ordered* is past perfect – the earlier action. So the album was already ordered while the show was still running; the show ended later.

questions.prompt: What is the past participle of «sing» – the form you need after «had»?
questions.explanation: The three forms are sing – sang – sung. After *had* you always need the past participle: «She had sung the song many times before.» *Sang* is the past simple, and *singed* is not a form of *sing*.
